author.name: Lewis Carroll
author.biography: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, a mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford. His fiction makes wordplay and logical puzzles part of ordinary conversation: a question about directions or an invitation to tea can become an argument about what words mean. Published in 1865, Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland follows a child who keeps asking questions even when the answers leave her more puzzled.

hook.text: How do you make sense of a world that keeps changing the rules?

paragraphs: Alice is bored by a book without pictures or conversations. Then a White Rabbit runs past, takes a watch from his waistcoat pocket and hurries away. She follows because she wants to know more. Curiosity gives her a direction before she has any idea where she is going.

Once she is down the rabbit-hole, familiar resources become unreliable. The verses she remembers will not come out right. Her body changes size. Polite questions draw impatient replies, and creatures who seem certain of the rules are rarely willing to explain them.

Carroll builds these encounters out of very particular misunderstandings. Listen for a word used in two senses, a question answered too literally, or a rule that serves only the person announcing it. Alice can be sharp and resourceful, but she also brings assumptions that other creatures have good reason to dislike.

The twelve chapters move through conversations, songs, games and interrupted stories. Let the nonsense unfold at its own pace. Alice’s wish to understand makes even a conversation that goes nowhere worth following.

orientation.text: Follow Alice through twelve chapters in order. Poems and songs belong to the action; notice how their words echo or disrupt the conversations around them.
